title: Shortness of Breath After Drinking: Causes and When to Worry
excerpt: Why you feel short of breath after drinking or the next day: sulfite and histamine asthma triggers, the flush reaction, hangxiety, reflux, heart rhythm, and when to call 911.
metaDescription: Short of breath after drinking? Sulfites, histamine, flush reactions, hangover anxiety, and heart rhythm causes, plus the warning signs that need 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**Call 911 first if this is happening right now:** if you or someone you're with is struggling to breathe after drinking, especially with **wheezing that won't settle, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, hives, chest pain or pressure, blue or gray lips, confusion, or breathing that is very slow, shallow, or irregular**, call 911 (or your local emergency number) now. If the person has passed out and can't be woken, turn them on their side so they can't choke, and stay with them. Those are signs of a severe allergic reaction, a heart problem, or alcohol poisoning, and none of them should be slept off. The rest of this page can wait.

**The honest answer, once you're safe:** for most social drinkers, feeling short of breath after drinking comes from one of a handful of common, manageable causes. The biggest one is a reaction to something in the drink, such as sulfites in wine or histamine in wine and beer, which can tighten the airways in people with asthma or sensitive airways. Other frequent causes are the flush reaction that some people get from acetaldehyde (a toxic breakdown product of alcohol), next-day anxiety that makes you over-breathe, acid reflux creeping up toward the throat, and a heart that's beating fast or out of rhythm after a big night. Less often, shortness of breath is a sign of something more serious. This guide walks through each cause, how to tell them apart, what helps, and when to get checked.

> **When to see a doctor or call 911:** **Call 911 right away** for trouble breathing with swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, hives spreading over the body, or a feeling of throat closing (possible anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction); wheezing that your rescue inhaler doesn't fix within minutes; chest pain or pressure, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, or fainting; blue or gray lips or fingertips; or someone who is very drunk with slow (fewer than about eight breaths a minute) or irregular breathing, cold clammy skin, or who can't be woken. **Book a doctor's appointment soon** if you get short of breath every time you drink, even after small amounts; if one type of drink reliably sets off wheezing or a stuffy nose; if you get winded more easily in daily life, have swollen ankles, or need to prop yourself up on pillows to breathe at night; or if you drink most days and notice shakiness, sweating, and a racing heart when you stop. That last pattern can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which is a medical issue a doctor can help with safely. This page is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Can Alcohol Make You Short of Breath?

Alcohol itself isn't usually what tightens your chest. It's a mix of what's in the glass, how your body processes it, and what drinking does to your heart, stomach, and nervous system. The main causes break down like this:

| Likely cause | How it tends to feel | Common clues |
|---|---|---|
| Sulfite or histamine reaction | Wheezing, tight chest, cough, stuffy or runny nose | Worse with wine (often white or sparkling) or certain beers; you have asthma or allergies |
| Flush reaction (acetaldehyde) | Red face, warm skin, fast heartbeat, chest tightness | Starts within minutes of the first drink; common in people of East Asian descent |
| Aspirin-sensitive asthma (AERD) | Wheezing and very blocked nose after even a few sips | You have asthma, nasal polyps, and react to aspirin or ibuprofen |
| Anxiety or panic the next day | Can't get a satisfying breath, sighing, tingling hands | Racing thoughts, dread, worse when you focus on it |
| Acid reflux | Burning chest, cough, hoarse voice, throat tightness | Worse lying down, after heavy drinking and late meals |
| Fast or irregular heartbeat | Pounding or fluttering heart, breathlessness, lightheadedness | After a binge; heart doesn't settle with rest |
| Breathing problems during sleep | Waking up gasping, loud snoring, morning headache | Worse on drinking nights; partner notices pauses |
| Alcohol poisoning | Slow, shallow, or irregular breathing, can't be woken | Lots of alcohol in a short time; this is an emergency |

The sections below take each one in turn.

## Sulfites, Histamine, and Alcohol-Triggered Asthma

If you have asthma, hay fever, or a history of a twitchy chest, the most likely reason for shortness of breath after drinking is a reaction to something in the drink rather than the alcohol. This is well recognized by allergists. An Australian questionnaire study of adults with asthma, published in the *Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology* around 2000, found that roughly a third reported alcoholic drinks had set off their asthma at least once, and wine was the drink blamed most often. Reactions usually came on quickly, within an hour, and were mostly mild to moderate.

### Sulfites

Sulfites (sulfur dioxide and related compounds) are preservatives that winemakers add to stop spoilage and oxidation. They also show up in some beers, ciders, and dried fruit. When you swallow a sulfite-containing drink, a small amount of sulfur dioxide gas is released and breathed in, and in sensitive people that gas irritates the airways and makes them narrow. That's why the reaction can happen within minutes.

A few useful facts:

- In the US, drinks with more than 10 parts per million of sulfites must say "contains sulfites" on the label, so nearly all wine does.
- White wines, sweet dessert wines, and some sparkling wines often carry more added sulfite than dry red wines, because red wine's natural tannins help preserve it.
- Sulfite sensitivity is uncommon in the general population and much more common in people with asthma, especially asthma that is harder to control.
- Sulfites are a common suspect for headaches, but the evidence there is weak. Breathing reactions in people with asthma are the part that holds up best. Our guide to [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) covers the headache side in more detail.

### Histamine

Wine (especially red), beer, and other fermented drinks contain histamine, the same chemical your body releases in an allergic reaction. Alcohol also slows the enzyme that breaks histamine down in your gut and may encourage your own cells to release more. In some people, the result is a stuffy or runny nose, flushing, itching, and, in those with sensitive airways, chest tightness and wheeze. If you also get a blocked nose, itchy skin, or headaches from aged cheese and cured meats, [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) is worth reading.

### What helps

- **Notice the pattern.** Write down what you drank and how you felt. Many people find one category, such as white wine, prosecco, or a particular beer, is the trigger while spirits mixed with plain soda don't bother them.
- **Have your inhaler with you** if you have asthma, and use it as your doctor has told you if symptoms start. If it doesn't help within minutes, treat that as an emergency.
- **Talk to your doctor or an allergist** if a drink reliably triggers wheezing. They can confirm whether sulfites or histamine are the culprit and adjust your asthma plan.
- **Don't rely on "sulfite-free" or "natural" wine as a guarantee.** All wine contains some naturally produced sulfites, and histamine levels vary by bottle.

## Aspirin-Sensitive Asthma (AERD): The Strongest Reactions

A specific condition called aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD, sometimes called Samter's triad) deserves its own mention. People with AERD have asthma, recurring nasal polyps, and breathing reactions to aspirin and similar painkillers like ibuprofen and naproxen. Studies of people with AERD have found that a large majority also report breathing or nasal symptoms after alcohol, sometimes after only a few sips, and of any type of drink.

If you have asthma and nasal polyps and drinking makes your nose block up and your chest tighten fast, ask your doctor about AERD. It's under-diagnosed, and getting the right diagnosis changes treatment. It's also another reason to be careful with hangover painkillers if you have asthma. Our guide to [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) covers the stomach side of that combination.

## The Flush Reaction: When Your Body Can't Clear Acetaldehyde

Your liver breaks alcohol down in two steps. First it turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, and then an enzyme called ALDH2 turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate. Many people of East Asian descent carry a gene variant that makes ALDH2 work poorly, so acetaldehyde builds up. The visible sign is the "Asian flush," a red face and neck, but acetaldehyde also widens blood vessels, speeds up your heart, and triggers histamine release.

Research from Japan, where this variant is common, has shown that in people with asthma who carry it, drinking can narrow the airways and bring on asthma attacks, and that acetaldehyde appears to be the main driver. So if your face goes red and your chest gets tight after one drink, the two are probably connected. The [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) guide explains the flush itself, and [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) covers how it differs from an allergy.

Some people take antihistamines to hide the flush. That can make the redness fade, but it doesn't stop acetaldehyde from building up, so it hides the warning sign without removing the cause. If you flush and get short of breath, the most effective step is drinking less, or not at all.

## Is It an Allergy? When Shortness of Breath Is an Emergency

True allergy to alcohol itself is extremely rare. Allergy to ingredients in drinks is less rare: grapes, wheat, barley, hops, yeast, egg or fish products used to clarify some wines and beers, nuts in liqueurs, or fruit in ciders and cocktails. Alcohol can also make an allergic reaction to food stronger, because it speeds up how fast allergens are absorbed. Some people only react to a food when they eat it with alcohol or around exercise.

The signs that a reaction may be anaphylaxis, a severe whole-body allergic reaction, are:

- Swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat
- A feeling of the throat closing, trouble swallowing, or a hoarse voice
- Wheezing or noisy, difficult breathing
- Hives or itching spreading across the body
- Feeling faint, dizzy, or suddenly very unwell, with vomiting or cramping

If any of these appear together after a drink, call 911. If the person has a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it as directed. Don't wait to see if it passes. Our page on [alcohol allergy](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy) goes through ingredient allergies and testing in more detail.

## Hangover Shortness of Breath: Why You Feel Winded the Next Day

A lot of people search for "hangover shortness of breath" because the breathless feeling shows up the morning after, not during the night out. Several things can pile up to cause it.

### Anxiety and over-breathing

Next-day anxiety, sometimes called hangxiety, is very common. As alcohol wears off, your brain swings from being calmed to being on edge, and stress hormones rise. Anxious people tend to breathe fast and shallow or keep taking big sighing breaths, which blows off too much carbon dioxide. That can cause a feeling of not getting enough air, tingling in your hands or lips, lightheadedness, and chest tightness. It feels frightening, but it isn't dangerous in itself. A useful clue is that the feeling gets worse when you focus on it and better when you're distracted.

Try slow breathing: breathe in through your nose for about four seconds, then out gently for about six, for a few minutes. If the breathlessness came with a racing heart and sense of doom, our guide to [panic attacks after drinking](/never-hungover/panic-attack-after-drinking) explains what's going on.

### A heart that hasn't settled

Alcohol raises your heart rate, and a heavy night can trigger extra beats or an irregular rhythm, most often atrial fibrillation, in otherwise healthy people. Doctors call this "holiday heart syndrome" because it tends to show up after weekends and holidays. When the heart beats fast or out of rhythm, it pumps less efficiently, and you can feel breathless, tired, and lightheaded. Most episodes settle on their own within a day, but an irregular rhythm needs a medical check because atrial fibrillation raises the risk of stroke. If your heart is pounding or fluttering along with the breathlessness, read [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).

### Dehydration and poor sleep

Alcohol makes you pee more, and vomiting or sweating on a dance floor adds to the fluid loss. Being dehydrated lowers your blood volume, so your heart beats faster to keep up, which can make you feel winded climbing stairs. Alcohol also breaks up deep sleep, so you wake up tired and every effort feels harder. These feelings are real but mild, and they ease as you rehydrate and rest. Our guide on whether [alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains how much fluid you actually lose.

### Reflux and a raw throat

Alcohol relaxes the muscle at the top of your stomach, letting acid creep up. Some of it can reach the throat and even get breathed in in small amounts, especially when you lie down drunk. That can cause a burning chest, coughing, a hoarse voice, and a tight, wheezy feeling, and acid reflux is a known asthma trigger in its own right. Vomiting can also irritate the throat and strain the muscles between your ribs, making deep breaths sore. [Heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) has practical tips.

## Breathing Problems While You Sleep After Drinking

Alcohol relaxes the muscles of your throat and dulls the brain's drive to breathe. In people who snore or have sleep apnea, this makes the airway collapse more often during sleep, causing pauses in breathing and drops in oxygen. You might wake up suddenly gasping or choking, with a pounding heart, then feel exhausted and headachy in the morning. Partners often notice loud snoring and silent pauses on drinking nights.

If that sounds familiar, stopping drinking for a few hours before bed helps, and it's worth asking your doctor about a sleep study, because untreated sleep apnea strains the heart over time. See [alcohol and sleep apnea](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-sleep-apnea) for more.

## Alcohol Poisoning: When Breathing Slows Down

This is the most dangerous cause, and it's the one where the person usually isn't the one noticing. Large amounts of alcohol in a short time can depress the part of the brain that controls breathing. Signs of alcohol poisoning include:

- Slow breathing (fewer than about eight breaths a minute) or gaps of ten seconds or more between breaths
- Confusion, stupor, or being impossible to wake
- Vomiting while drowsy or unconscious
- Seizures
- Cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin
- Very low body temperature

If you see these, call 911. Turn the person onto their side so they can't choke on vomit, keep them warm, and stay with them. Don't give coffee or a cold shower, and don't let them "sleep it off." Blood alcohol can keep rising after the last drink, so someone who seems only very drunk can get worse.

## Wine, Beer, or Spirits: Does the Drink Matter?

For breathing symptoms, the type of drink often matters more than the amount of alcohol.

- **Wine** is the drink most often linked to asthma symptoms. It can carry sulfites, histamine, and other compounds formed during fermentation. White and sparkling wines are frequently blamed because of their added sulfites. Red wine tends to carry more histamine.
- **Beer and cider** can contain histamine, sulfites (in some brands), and grain or hop proteins that a small number of people are allergic to. If you react to beer but not wine, a wheat, barley, or hop allergy is worth considering, and [gluten-free alcohol](/never-hungover/gluten-free-alcohol) lists options if gluten is the concern.
- **Clear spirits** like vodka and gin mixed with plain soda water are generally the lowest in sulfites and histamine, though cocktail mixers, cordials, and fruit can add triggers back in.

None of this makes any drink "safe" for everyone. It's a starting point for working out your own pattern.

## Shortness of Breath From Regular Heavy Drinking

If you drink heavily most days over months or years, new breathlessness deserves a proper look. Long-term heavy drinking can weaken the heart muscle (alcoholic cardiomyopathy), which shows up as getting winded on exertion, swelling in the ankles, a cough when lying flat, and waking up breathless at night. Heavy drinking also raises the risk of pneumonia, partly because it weakens the lungs' defenses and partly because of inhaled vomit, and it often goes along with smoking, which damages the lungs directly.

These aren't hangover problems. They're signs that your heart or lungs need checking, and a doctor can do that with simple tests like a chest X-ray, an ECG (a recording of your heart's electrical activity), and blood tests. If you drink daily and notice shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or feeling very anxious when you go without, tell your doctor. That can be alcohol withdrawal, and stopping suddenly without help can be risky, so it's best managed with medical support.

## What to Do Right Now If You Feel Short of Breath After Drinking

If none of the emergency signs apply and you feel mildly winded or tight-chested:

1. **Stop drinking.** Whatever started it will likely get worse with more.
2. **Sit upright.** Lying flat makes reflux and breathing harder. Lean slightly forward with your hands on your knees if that's comfortable.
3. **Use your reliever inhaler** if you have asthma, as prescribed. If it doesn't help within a few minutes, or you need it again soon after, call 911.
4. **Slow your breathing.** In through your nose for four seconds, out for six. This helps most with anxiety-driven breathlessness.
5. **Sip water.** Small sips, not gulps, especially if you've been vomiting.
6. **Loosen tight clothing** and get some fresh, cool air.
7. **Check your pulse.** If it's very fast, irregular, or won't settle after 15 to 20 minutes of rest, get medical help.
8. **Don't be alone.** Tell someone how you feel so they can call for help if it gets worse.

Avoid using sleeping pills, sedating antihistamines, or anxiety medication to calm down after drinking. They add to alcohol's effect on your breathing. Our guides to [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) and [anxiety medication and alcohol](/never-hungover/anxiety-medication-and-alcohol) explain why.

## What a Doctor Might Check

If you see a doctor about breathlessness linked to drinking, expect questions about which drinks set it off, how fast it starts, your asthma and allergy history, any reaction to aspirin or ibuprofen, your heart rhythm, and how much you usually drink. Depending on what they hear, they might:

- Listen to your chest and check your oxygen level
- Order breathing tests (spirometry) to look for asthma
- Arrange allergy testing for drink ingredients
- Do an ECG, or give you a monitor to wear, if a rhythm problem is suspected
- Suggest a sleep study if sleep apnea seems likely
- Order a chest X-ray or blood tests if heart or lung disease is a concern

Be honest about how much you drink. Doctors ask because it changes what they look for, not to judge you.

## How to Lower the Odds Next Time

- **Find your trigger drink and skip it.** For many people, swapping white wine or prosecco for a clear spirit with soda makes a big difference.
- **Keep your asthma well controlled** day to day. People whose asthma is poorly controlled react more to sulfites and other triggers.
- **Carry your inhaler** on nights out, and any epinephrine auto-injector you've been prescribed.
- **Drink less and more slowly.** Lower peaks in blood alcohol mean less acetaldehyde, a calmer heart, and less reflux. Alternating each drink with a glass of water helps.
- **Eat before and while drinking**, and avoid lying down right after a big meal and several drinks.
- **Stop drinking a few hours before bed**, especially if you snore.
- **Don't smoke or vape while drinking.** It adds airway irritation on top of everything else.

You may see DHM (dihydromyricetin) supplements mentioned for drinking nights. DHM has been studied mainly in animals for alcohol and acetaldehyde clearance, and there is no good evidence that it prevents asthma reactions, sulfite sensitivity, allergic reactions, or alcohol-related heart rhythm problems. It doesn't replace your inhaler, an allergy plan, or a doctor's assessment, so we don't recommend any supplement for this symptom. Finding and avoiding your trigger drink, and getting checked if breathing trouble keeps happening, is what actually helps.

## The Bottom Line

Shortness of breath after drinking is usually a reaction to something in the drink, such as sulfites or histamine, the flush reaction, next-day anxiety, reflux, or a heart that's been pushed too hard for a night. Most of these ease with rest, an inhaler if you have asthma, and avoiding your trigger drink. But breathing trouble with swelling, hives, chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, or very slow breathing in someone who's drunk is an emergency, so call 911. And if it happens every time you drink, or you're getting winded more in daily life, see a doctor so you know what's really causing it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get short of breath after drinking alcohol?**

The most common reasons are a reaction to sulfites or histamine in the drink (especially if you have asthma), the flush reaction from acetaldehyde building up, next-day anxiety that makes you over-breathe, acid reflux, and a fast or irregular heartbeat after heavy drinking. Rarely it can be a severe allergic reaction or, in someone very drunk, alcohol poisoning slowing their breathing. Swelling, hives, chest pain, or very slow breathing need 911.

**Is hangover shortness of breath normal?**

Feeling a bit winded the day after drinking is common and usually comes from dehydration, poor sleep, a faster heart rate, and anxiety. It should ease as you rest and rehydrate. It isn't normal to struggle to breathe, wheeze, have chest pain, or feel your heart racing irregularly. Those need medical attention, and if they're severe, call 911.

**Can alcohol trigger asthma?**

Yes. Surveys of people with asthma have found that many report alcoholic drinks have triggered their symptoms at least once, with wine blamed most often. Sulfites, histamine, and acetaldehyde are the main suspects. People with aspirin-sensitive asthma (AERD) often react to small amounts of any drink. If drinking sets off your asthma, talk to your doctor about your asthma plan and carry your inhaler.

**Why does wine make me short of breath but not vodka?**

Wine usually contains added sulfites and more histamine than clear spirits, and both can tighten the airways in sensitive people. Vodka mixed with plain soda water is generally low in both. That pattern points toward a sulfite or histamine reaction rather than a problem with alcohol itself, which is worth mentioning to your doctor or an allergist.

**Can anxiety after drinking make it hard to breathe?**

Yes. Next-day anxiety often causes fast, shallow breathing or repeated sighing, which can make you feel like you can't get a full breath, along with tingling hands, lightheadedness, and chest tightness. Slow breathing, in for four seconds and out for six, usually helps. If the feeling doesn't ease, or comes with chest pain or an irregular heartbeat, get checked.

**When is shortness of breath after drinking an emergency?**

Call 911 for trouble breathing with swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, spreading hives, wheezing your inhaler doesn't fix, chest pain or pressure, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, fainting, blue lips, or someone who is very drunk with slow or irregular breathing or who can't be woken.

**Can drinking cause shortness of breath when lying down?**

Lying down after drinking can make reflux worse, which can cause coughing and a tight chest, and alcohol makes snoring and sleep apnea worse, so you may wake up gasping. If you regularly need to prop yourself up on pillows to breathe, or wake up breathless at night even without drinking, see a doctor, because that can be a sign of a heart problem.

**Does DHM help with shortness of breath after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats breathing problems after drinking, including asthma, sulfite or histamine reactions, or allergic reactions. Its research focuses on alcohol metabolism and is mostly in animals. If drinking makes you short of breath, avoiding your trigger drink and talking to your doctor will do far more than any supplement.
